::: {.lead}
*Night Owl Games* has the script of the opening scene of *Rooftop Rescue*
(lecture 7). Before the artists build the flooded street and the animators
move Nour's boat, the team wants to **see** the scene: what the camera shows
first, how close it comes to Salma, and how one shot follows another. They
draw a **storyboard**: a row of simple pictures, one for each shot. In
lectures 3 to 8 you wrote the story and the scene. In this lesson you plan
the pictures: you choose the shot, place things in the frame, and keep the
flow clear from panel to panel. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary storyboard panel panel-caption shot wide-shot medium-shot close-up camera-angle composition rule-of-thirds lead-room screen-direction 180-degree-rule >}}

## 9.1 See the scene before you build it: the storyboard

Building one shot of a 3D cutscene can take a team days: the place, the
characters, the animation, the light. If the shot is wrong, the work is
lost. A drawing takes two minutes. So the team draws first (@fig-board).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.1 — Storyboard"}
A **storyboard** is a series of simple drawings, called **panels**, that
shows shot by shot what the camera will show in a scene. Under each panel, a
**caption** gives the action, the dialogue or sound, and the time.
:::

![A storyboard of the opening of *Rooftop Rescue*: four panels, each with its notes.](images/storyboard-page.png){#fig-board width=96%}

A storyboard is not art. Stick figures and boxes are fine, because the
board must answer only three questions: what does the player see, what
happens, and how long does it take? Games use storyboards for cutscenes,
trailers and also for gameplay moments, such as the first time the player
meets a boss (lecture 11).

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.1 — From script to panels"}
The script says: "EXT. FLOODED STREET – DUSK. Nour jumps into the boat.
NOUR: Hold on, everyone."

1. Panel 1 shows the place: the flooded street. Caption: "Wide: the street
   at dusk. SFX: water, wind. 3 s."
2. Panel 2 shows the action: Nour jumps into the boat. "SFX: splash. 2 s."
3. Panel 3 shows the line: Nour's face. "NOUR: Hold on, everyone. 2 s."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Drawing beautiful panels. A storyboard is a plan, not the final art: if one
panel takes twenty minutes, nobody wants to change it. Use simple shapes.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Three panels on paper"}
Fold an A4 paper twice to get four boxes. Use three of them.

1. Draw the first three panels of the script in Example 9.1 with simple
   shapes.
2. Under each panel, write the action or the line, a sound and a time.

*Your result:* three panels with captions.
:::

## 9.2 How close is the camera? Shot sizes

The same moment can be shown from far or from near. Each **shot size**
tells the player something different (@fig-sizes).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.2 — Shot sizes"}
A **wide shot** shows the whole place, with the characters small in it; the
first wide shot of a scene is the **establishing shot**. A **medium shot**
shows a character from about the waist up. A **close-up** fills the frame
with a face or one object.
:::

![Three shot sizes: the wide shot answers "where?", the medium shot "what?", the close-up "how does it feel?".](images/shot-sizes.png){#fig-sizes width=96%}

| Shot size | What the player learns | Rooftop Rescue |
|---|---|---|
| Wide (establishing) | where the scene happens | the flooded street at dusk |
| Medium | what a character does | Nour rows the boat |
| Close-up | what a character feels, or an important detail | Salma's fear; the cat |

: Shot sizes and what they show. {#tbl-sizes}

The **camera angle** changes the feeling too: from above (a high angle), a
character looks small and weak; from below (a low angle), big and strong.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.2 — Choosing the size for each beat"}
1. The scene starts: the player does not know the place. **Wide shot.**
2. Nour rows hard against the water: an action. **Medium shot.**
3. Salma says "I won't leave without my cat." The line is about fear:
   **close-up**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using the same size for every panel. A board of only medium shots never
shows the place and never shows a feeling. Change the size when the purpose
changes.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Three sizes with your phone"}
Choose one object on your desk (a bottle, a bag).

1. With the camera of your phone, take a wide shot (the object small, the
   room around it), a medium shot and a close-up.
2. Under each photo, write what the player would learn from it.

*Your result:* three photos and three sentences.
:::

## 9.3 Where does the eye go? Composition

Nour rows to the right. In the first draft, the artist put her at the right
edge of the frame: the boat seems to hit the border. Moving her to the left
gives the player room to look where she goes (@fig-thirds).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.3 — Rule of thirds and lead room"}
**Composition** is the way things are placed in the frame. The **rule of
thirds**: two lines across and two lines down split the frame into thirds,
and the main subject goes on a line or where two lines meet. **Lead room** is
empty space in front of a character, in the direction it looks or moves.
:::

![On the left third, Nour has lead room; at the right edge, she has none.](images/thirds.png){#fig-thirds width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.3 — Placing Nour"}
The frame is 16 units wide. The thirds lines are at about 5.3 and 10.7.

1. Nour rows to the right, so she goes on the **left** line (about 5.3).
2. The 10 units in front of her are lead room: the player looks there, to
   where she goes.
3. On the roof, Salma looks to the left, so she goes on the **right** line.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Putting every subject in the exact centre. A centred subject looks still and
leaves no room for movement. Use the thirds lines, and keep the lead room in
front.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/frame-lab.html" poster="sims/frame-lab.png" title="Frame Lab: shot size and composition with a camera" height="660" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Thirds on your phone"}
Turn on the grid of your phone camera (Android: camera settings › Grid
lines; iPhone: Settings › Camera › Grid). Or use **Frame Lab** above.

1. Take a photo of a person or a toy that "looks" to one side. Put it on a
   thirds line, with lead room in front.
2. Take a second photo with the subject at the edge, looking out of the
   frame. Which one feels better? Why?

*Your result:* two photos and one sentence.
:::

## 9.4 From panel to panel: flow and the 180-degree rule

In panel 2, Nour rows from left to right. In panel 4 the artist drew her from
the other side of the street: now she rows from right to left. The player
thinks she turned back. The **screen direction** changed (@fig-180).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.4 — The 180-degree rule"}
Draw an imagined line through the action (the **line of action**: here,
Nour's path). The **180-degree rule** says: keep the camera on **one side**
of this line. Then characters keep their place on the screen, and a
movement keeps its **screen direction** from panel to panel.
:::

![Seen from above: cameras A and B are on one side of the line, camera C on the other. From C, Nour seems to row back.](images/line-180.png){#fig-180 width=96%}

Arrows in the panels show movement, so the reader of the board sees the
direction at once. Panels are numbered, and each one leads to the next:
place, then action, then feeling.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.4 — Checking the direction"}
1. Panels 2 and 3: Nour rows left to right in both. Right.
2. Panel 4 was drawn from camera C: she rows right to left. Wrong.
3. Fix: draw panel 4 from camera B, on the same side of the line.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that only films need continuity. A game cutscene that flips the
direction makes the player lose the way, and so does a gameplay camera that
jumps to the other side of the line.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Arrows and the line"}
Take your three panels of section 9.1.

1. Draw an arrow for every movement.
2. Draw the line of action on a small map from above, and mark where your
   camera stands for each panel. Are all cameras on one side?

*Your result:* panels with arrows and a small map with the line and the
cameras.
:::

## Case study: storyboarding Rooftop Rescue

*Night Owl Games* storyboards the opening of *Rooftop Rescue*. The beats are:
the flooded street at dusk; Nour jumps into the boat and rows towards the
roof; Nour says "Hold on, everyone. I'm coming."; Nour rows on; and on the
roof Salma says "I won't leave without my cat." Nour rows from left to
right, and the camera stays on one side of her path. The board must show the
place first, the actions in medium shots, and the feelings in close-ups. The
Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses this scene. In the mini-game
below you call the shot for each panel.

{{< sim file="sims/shot-caller.html" poster="sims/shot-caller.png" title="Shot Caller: choose the shot for each panel" kind="game" height="700" >}}

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., the chapters on story and on
indirect control (how the camera and the frame guide the player). Many free
storyboard templates (16:9 frames with caption lines) can be printed from
the web.

## Exercises

1. What is a storyboard? Why does a team draw one before it builds a scene?
2. What does the caption of a panel give?
3. Which shot size shows where a scene happens?
4. Which shot size do you use for a character's fear? Why?
5. Nour rows hard against the water. Which shot size shows this action best?
6. What does a low camera angle say about a character?
7. What is the rule of thirds?
8. A character walks to the left. On which thirds line do you place it, and
   why?
9. What is the 180-degree rule? What goes wrong when a panel breaks it?
10. *Rooftop Rescue*: write the shot size of the four beats: the street; Nour
    rows; Nour's line; Salma's line.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. A series of simple drawings that shows shot by shot what the camera shows; a drawing is cheap to change, a built shot is not.
2. The action, the dialogue or sound, and the time.
3. The wide (establishing) shot.
4. A close-up: the face shows the feeling.
5. A medium shot.
6. The character looks big and strong.
7. Two lines across and two down split the frame into thirds; the subject goes on a line or where two lines meet.
8. On the right line, so that the lead room is on the left, in front of it.
9. The camera stays on one side of the line of action; if a panel breaks it, the screen direction flips and the player thinks the character turned back.
10. Wide; medium; close-up of Nour; close-up of Salma.
:::
